name: Feminism
summary: Feminism is a family of movements and theories that seek equality of the sexes in political, economic, personal and social life. It holds that societies have been organized in ways that favor men, and works to end that through legal reform, challenges to gender roles and stereotypes, reproductive rights and protection from violence. Liberal, socialist, radical and intersectional strands differ on how deep the change must go and on issues such as sex work.
scope: The mainstream of contemporary feminism, drawing on the liberal, socialist/materialist, radical and intersectional strands as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy describes them, with the Declaration of Sentiments (Seneca Falls, 1848), Wollstonecraft's Vindication (1792), Mill's Subjection of Women (1869) and the Combahee River Collective Statement (1977, the intersectional strand) as primary texts. A position is recorded only where these sources state it as feminist; where strands differ without a source taking a side, the answer is null. Trans-exclusionary radical feminism and anti-feminist currents are not followed.

notes: Feminism is a broad family and its defining sources state positions mainly on sex equality, marriage, property, the vote, gender, reproduction and intersecting oppressions. Later pass (2026-11-13, rules 7): every earlier answer was re-checked against the saved sources (Wikipedia, six Stanford Encyclopedia entries, the Declaration of Sentiments, Wollstonecraft, Mill, the Combahee statement). 191 answers resting on adherents' views, general values or Wikipedia alone were nulled and 19 were re-sourced. Themes searched without finding a stated position: economy and markets, taxation, welfare and basic income, government and constitutions, the military and war, violence, immigration and borders, ecology, technology, speech and pornography, religion in the state, and foreign policy. Gilman's The Man-Made World and Stanton's Eighty Years and More were read but not cited, because the defining sources do not tie them to the ideology by title. CEDAW and the Beijing Platform were not retrievable (403 from the UN and OHCHR sites, which stay refused). Sex work is a documented split (0, low); the uncertainty rule fails because the record says little on economic, constitutional and foreign-policy lines.
